Japan’s 7th Strategic Energy Plan (Approved February 2025)
This is the core policy document, issued by the Cabinet and led by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) / Agency for Natural Resources and Energy (ANRE). It sets targets for FY2040 while aiming for carbon neutrality by 2050:
Nuclear power: Target ~20% of electricity generation (up from ~8.5% in FY2023). The plan explicitly shifts from "reducing dependence as much as possible" (post-Fukushima language) to "maximizing" use.
Renewables: Main power source, targeted at 40–50% (from ~20% currently).
Fossil fuels (thermal): Reduced to 30–40% (from ~70%).
Overall approach: Prioritizes safety while treating nuclear as essential baseload power amid rising electricity demand (driven by AI/data centers, digitalization, etc.).
Key measures to achieve the nuclear target include:
Restarting existing reactors (with rigorous Nuclear Regulation Authority (NRA) safety reviews).
Extending operations of reactors beyond the "in principle" 40-year limit (with approvals for 20-year extensions possible after reviews).
Developing and deploying next-generation/advanced reactors (including replacement builds; new construction is now permitted for the first time since 2011).
Promoting the nuclear fuel cycle (reprocessing spent fuel).
Implementation and Progress (as of mid-2026)
Operating reactors: Around 15 reactors online (e.g., Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Unit 6 restarted commercially in early 2026, a major milestone as TEPCO's first post-Fukushima restart at the world's largest plant). More restarts are underway or approved (e.g., Tomari-3 expected ~2027).
Challenges: Regulatory hurdles, local approvals, anti-terrorism/seismic upgrades, and some delays/falsification issues. Not all 33+ operable reactors are running; capacity 
Japanese leadership recognized by the late 1940s that nuclear was the future and started funding the development of technologies  for extracting uranium from seawater. This development continues today and their engineers have had success but their technology is not economically viable yet.
